title: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Slow accumulated change hides the wild parents of old cultivated plants

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because a large amount of change has been slowly and unconsciously accumulated in long-cultivated plants, in many cases their wild parent-stocks can no longer be recognised.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: A large amount of change in our cultivated plants, thus slowly and unconsciously accumulated, explains, as I believe, the well-known fact, that in a vast number of cases we cannot recognise, and therefore do not know, the wild parent-stocks of the plants which have been longest cultivated in our flower and kitchen gardens.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Unknown Origin of our Domestic Productions”. Scope: long-cultivated garden and crop plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Crop genomics can now infer many parent stocks and quantify divergence, but cannot cleanly recover nineteenth-century recognizability or exclude lost ancestors. The proposed causal explanation is therefore only partly testable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across long-cultivated plants, relate genomic and morphological divergence from inferred wild relatives to whether parent stocks were historically recognizable, controlling extinction and sampling. Greater accumulated change associated with failed recognition supports the explanation.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Modern genomics can identify parents once unrecognizable morphologically.

Extinction and unsampled wild diversity are rival explanations.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.56
analysis feasibility: 0.67
data adequacy: 0.61
data existence: 0.82
operationalizability: 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Crop wild-relative databases and floras now record progenitor status for a large set of long-cultivated plants, and sequence archives can supply distances for the staples. That is enough to test recognizability as a present-day fact and to compare it with divergence for well-studied crops. Extinction, hybridization, and thin coverage of ornamental garden plants keep the causal story, accumulated change as the reason parents are unknown, only partly identified.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For plants with the longest cultivation histories, score whether a wild progenitor is identified and measure genomic or phenotypic distance to the nearest wild relative. The explanatory claim would be supported if unidentified progenitors were exactly the most diverged stocks; it would be weakened if large divergence still left progenitors identifiable, or if unidentified parents were mostly extinct or unsampled rather than unrecognizably modified.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Minor garden plants are far less completely linked to wild relatives than major staples.

Hybrid origins create several partial parents rather than one unrecognizable stock.

A wild parent may be unrecognizable because it is extinct or uncollected, not because the crop changed.
